en: The Questions of Milinda:
The Chapter on the All-Knowing Wisdom within the Section of Puzzling Questions.

7. The Question on Wholesome and Unwholesome Actions, Equal or Unequal “Venerable Nāgasena, is the ripening of one who performs wholesome deeds and one who performs unwholesome deeds equal and the same, or is there some distinction?

“There is, Great King, a distinction between the wholesome and the unwholesome. The wholesome, Great King, has a pleasant ripening and leads to heaven; the unwholesome has a painful ripening and leads to hell.”
“Venerable Nāgasena, you say:
‘Devadatta was entirely black, endowed with entirely black qualities; the Bodhisatta was entirely white, endowed with entirely white qualities.
Yet again, in birth after birth, Devadatta was equal to the Bodhisatta in fame and following, and sometimes even superior.”
When Devadatta was the son of the royal chaplain to King Brahmadatta in the city of Bārāṇasī, the Bodhisatta was a low-caste Caṇḍāla who was a master of spells;
having recited his incantations, he produced mango fruits out of season.
In this instance, the Bodhisatta was inferior to Devadatta both by birth and by reputation.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a king, a great lord of the earth endowed with all desirable things, the Bodhisatta was his state elephant, a noble tusker possessed of all auspicious marks.
Unable to endure the elephant’s graceful gait and charm, the king, desiring its death, spoke thus to the elephant trainer: "The elephant is not yet trained by you, teacher."
"Perform the feat called 'walking through the air,'" he said; even then, the Bodhisatta was inferior to Devadatta in birth, being lowly and an animal.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a human being who had lost his way in the forest, the Bodhisatta was the Great Earth.
There was a monkey by that name; even here, first of all, a distinction is seen between a human and an animal.
Even in that case, the Bodhisatta was inferior to Devadatta by birth.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a human being named Soṇuttara, a hunter who was powerful and more powerful still—
Nāgabala, at that time the Bodhisatta was the elephant king named Chaddanta;
then it was Devadatta who caused that noble elephant to be killed—there too, Devadatta was the greater offender.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a human being, a forest-dweller living without a fixed abode, at that time the Bodhisatta...
He was a partridge bird, a reciter of mantras; even then, that forest-dweller killed the bird, and even there, Devadatta alone was superior by birth.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was the King of Kāsi named Kalābu, the Bodhisatta was an ascetic.
He was a teacher of patience; at that time, the king, enraged by that ascetic, had his hands and feet cut off like bamboo joints.
Even then, Devadatta alone was superior in both birth and fame.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a human being living as a forest-dweller, the Bodhisatta was named Nandiya.
He was a lord of monkeys; even then, that forest-dweller killed that lord of monkeys along with his mother and younger brother, and even there, Devadatta alone was superior by birth.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a human being, an unclothed ascetic named Kārambhīya, the Bodhisatta was a king of nāgas named Paṇḍaraka; even there, Devadatta alone was superior by birth.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a human being, a matted-hair ascetic in the forest, the Bodhisatta was a great boar named Tacchaka; even then, Devadatta alone was superior by birth.

Furthermore, when Devadatta was a king among the Cetis named Sūraparicaro, who could travel through the air at a height of seven men, the Bodhisatta was a brahmin named Kapila; even then, Devadatta alone [was superior].
He was superior in both birth and fame.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a human named Sāma, the Bodhisatta was a king of deer named Ruru; even then, Devadatta alone was superior in birth.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a human who lived as a hunter in the forest, the Bodhisatta was a noble elephant.
There was a hunter who, having cut off the tusks of that noble elephant seven times, carried them away;
even there, Devadatta alone was superior by birth.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a jackal possessing the nature of a khattiya, he [ruled] over all the regional kings throughout Jambudīpa.
He made them all devoted to his service; at that time, the Bodhisatta was a wise man named Vidhura, and even then Devadatta alone was superior in fame.

Furthermore, when Devadatta, having become an elephant, killed the young ones of the Laṭukikā bird, the Bodhisatta was also an elephant, the leader of the herd; there, for the time being, they were both exactly equal.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a yakkha named Adhamma, the Bodhisatta was also a yakkha named Dhamma; even then, both were exactly equal.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a shipowner, the master of five hundred families, the Bodhisatta was also a shipowner, the master of five hundred families; even then, both were exactly equal.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a caravan leader, the master of five hundred wagons, at that time...
The Bodhisatta was also a caravan leader, the master of five hundred wagons; even then, the two of them were exactly equal.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a king of deer named Sākha, the Bodhisatta was also a king of deer named Nigrodha; even then, the two of them were exactly equal.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was a general named Sākha, the Bodhisatta was also a king named Nigrodha; even then, the two of them were exactly equal.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was the brahmin named Khaṇḍahāla, the Bodhisatta was a prince named Canda; at that time, Khaṇḍahāla himself was the superior one.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was the king named Brahmadatta, the Bodhisatta was his son, a prince named Mahāpaduma;
at that time, the king had his own son thrown down a thieves’ precipice. From that...
In some cases, a father is even more distinguished and superior to his sons; yet even there, Devadatta was the most superior.
Furthermore, when Devadatta was the king named Mahāpatāpa, the Bodhisatta was his son, the prince named Dhammapāla;
at that time, the king had his own son’s hands, feet, and head cut off.
Even there, Devadatta alone was superior and more eminent.
Recently, both were born into the Sakya clan.

The Bodhisatta became a Buddha, omniscient and a leader of the world; while Devadatta, having gone forth in the teaching of that God of Gods, manifested psychic power and made himself a rival to the Buddha.
“Venerable Nāgasena, is all that I have said true, or is it false?
“Great King, all the various reasons you have set forth are exactly so, and not otherwise.
“If, venerable Nāgasena, both the black and the white [karmas] have an identical destination, then surely wholesome and unwholesome deeds must have an identical ripening.”
“No indeed, Great King, neither the wholesome nor the unwholesome has an equal ripening. For it is not the case, Great King, that Devadatta was hostile toward all people;
he was hostile only toward the Bodhisatta. Whoever was hostile toward him because of the Bodhisatta, for that person alone does the fruit ripen in each respective existence.”

“Great King, even Devadatta, while established in sovereignty, provided protection for the countryside; he had bridges, assembly halls, and almshouses built; and he gave gifts as desired to ascetics and brahmins, to the poor, the destitute, and beggars, and to those with or without protectors.
By the result of that, he obtained prosperity in birth after birth.
Great King, who could say that one would experience such prosperity without giving, self-control, restraint, and the observance of the Uposatha?”
Furthermore, Great King, as for what you say— that Devadatta and the Bodhisatta revolved together—
it was not after the passing of a hundred births that their meeting occurred, nor after a thousand births, nor after a hundred thousand births; rather,
their meeting occurred only once in a great while, after the passing of many days and nights.
Furthermore, Great King, regarding this parable of the blind turtle taught by the Blessed One for the sake of obtaining human birth—know, Great King, that this meeting of ours is just like that.
It was not only with Devadatta, Great King, that the Bodhisatta had a meeting;
for throughout many hundreds of thousands of births, Great King, the Elder Sāriputta was the Bodhisatta’s father, his paternal grandfather, and his paternal uncle.
He was his brother; he was his son; he was his nephew; he was his friend.

And the Bodhisatta, O Great King, throughout many hundreds of thousands of births, was the father of the Elder Sāriputta, his grandfather, his great-grandfather, his brother, his son, his nephew, and his friend.
"Indeed, Great King, all beings included within the category of living beings, following the stream of saṃsāra and being carried along by that stream,
encounter both the unpleasant and the pleasant.
Just as water, Great King, being carried along by a current, encounters both the pure and the impure, the beautiful and the foul."

In the same way, Great King, all beings included within the realm of sentient existence follow the stream of *saṃsāra*; being carried along by that stream of *saṃsāra*, they encounter both the unpleasant and the pleasant.

Great King, Devadatta, while being a *yakṣa*, himself being unrighteous and inciting others to unrighteousness, suffered in the great hell for fifty-seven million and six hundred thousand years. And the Bodhisattva too, Great King, while being a *yakṣa*...
"Having established himself in the Dhamma and led others to the Dhamma, he rejoiced in heaven for seventy-five koṭis of years and six hundred thousand years, endowed with all his desires.
Yet, O Great King, Devadatta, having offended against the Buddha who is beyond offense in this very life and having split the harmonious Saṅgha, entered the earth;
whereas the Tathāgata, having awakened to all phenomena, has attained final Nibbāna in the destruction of the acquisitions."
“Excellent, venerable Nāgasena! It is so; thus do I accept it.
This was the seventh dilemma, concerning the wholesome and unwholesome, the even and the uneven.
